lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7 you made prototypes. What is a prototype? (An early model made to test an idea.) Today: invent a product with a sensor and a program, test it, and show it at an expo.

Start with a real problem and a real user. Interview them, watch what happens, and list their needs. Example: a family's plants dry out when they are away. The brief: an automatic plant waterer for a windowsill.
Plan it: a specification, and a systems diagram of the moisture sensor, the program and the pump. Add a parts list within a budget, and a Gantt chart for six weeks.
Build and program it: a flowchart first, then the code. Every minute it reads the soil; when the reading is below 30, the pump runs for 2 seconds.
Test it fairly and record each version in a table. Version 3 watered on time 18 of 20 times: 18 ÷ 20 = 0.9, so 90%. Repeat timings and work out the mean.
Improve the weakest part, test again, and keep a record of each version. Ask your user to try it, and listen carefully to what they say.
At the expo, your stand shows the problem, the product, a live demo and your results as a chart. Say what you would do next. Speak clearly, answer questions, and thank everyone who helped.

Try it in the world: build an expo stand in your village with a working machine. In LIFE, Talk & Deal practises a pitch: the problem, the idea, why you, what you need. The Tool Book's stopwatch times your tests. Next: a history documentary.

exercises.prompt: Put the invention steps in order.
items: find a problem and a user
write a brief and a plan
exercises.hint: You need a problem before a plan, and a product before an expo.
exercises.explain: Problem and user, brief and plan, build and program, test and improve, then the expo.

exercises.prompt: Which makes the best starting point for an invention?
choices: a real need of a real user
a copy of a shop product
exercises.explain: Inventions that solve a real person's real problem are the ones people use.

exercises.prompt: The waterer worked 18 times in 20 tests. What percentage is that?
exercises.hint: Divide the times it worked by the tests, then times 100.

exercises.prompt: A live demo shows the product working at the expo.
exercises.hint: What does 'live' mean on a stand?
exercises.explain: True: a live demo shows the invention really working, in front of the visitors.

exercises.prompt: Build the expo stand's floor: a rectangle of 12 squares with a perimeter of 14.
exercises.hint: Which two numbers multiply to 12 and add up to 7?

exercises.prompt: In which week does this plan finish?
exercises.hint: Find the bar that reaches furthest to the right.
exercises.explain: The expo stand ends in week 6, the last bar.

exercises.prompt: Five tests of how long the pump ran, in seconds: 9, 11, 10, 12 and 8. What is the mean?
exercises.hint: Add the five results, then divide by 5.

choices: the same pot, soil and water each time
exercises.hint: A fair test changes only one thing.
exercises.explain: Keeping the pot, soil and water the same means any change is down to the version being tested.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of the stand to its job.
exercises.hint: What should each part tell a visitor?
exercises.explain: The problem: why. The demo: it works. The chart: proof. Next steps: how it will get better.

exercises.hint: Would a visitor trust and enjoy it?
exercises.explain: Good: speaking clearly, honest results, thanks. Not good: reading every word, hiding what went wrong.

exercises.prompt: If version 2 worked 16 of 20 times, it was 80% reliable.
Version 1 worked 12 of 20 times and version 3 worked 18 of 20 times. By how many percentage points did it improve?
exercises.hint: Turn both into percentages first, then subtract.

exercises.prompt: The budget is 20 gold. The sensor costs 3, the pump 6, the battery box 2 and the case 4. How much is left?
exercises.hint: Add the parts, then take the total from the budget.

exercises.prompt: The pump sometimes floods the pot. What is the best improvement to test?
choices: pump for 1 second, then check again
exercises.hint: Which change gives less water and keeps checking?
exercises.explain: A shorter pump time with a re-check adds water in small amounts until the soil is damp, so it can't flood.

exercises.prompt: Which line makes the waterer wait a minute between checks?
exercises.hint: pause() counts in milliseconds: how many in a minute?
exercises.explain: 60,000 milliseconds = 60 seconds = 1 minute, so pause(60000) is the wait between checks.

exercises.prompt: The mean of several tests is more trustworthy than a single test.
exercises.hint: Could one test be a fluke?
exercises.explain: True: repeating tests and taking the mean evens out flukes.
